{{DISPLAYTITLE:Functions that always finish}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Structural and well-founded recursion}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Every function defined inside Lean's logic must finish: given any input, it must return an
answer after finitely many steps. This page says why that rule exists, how Lean checks it,
and what becomes of a program that might run for ever.

== Why a loop would be a proof ==

In Lean a definition is more than a recipe for computing. It is also an equation the logic
may use in proofs. Write a definition that says "the answer for n is the answer for n, plus
one", and you have asked the logic to accept that some number equals itself plus one. No
natural number does. If the equation were admitted, Lean could prove a false statement, and
from one false statement every statement follows. The whole system would be worthless.

So Lean refuses the definition:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def loop (n : Nat) : Nat := loop n + 1
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 begins its reply with <code>fail to show termination for</code>, names
<code>loop</code>, and gives its reason: the argument <code>n</code> "is unchanged in the
recursive calls". Nothing gets smaller, so nothing guarantees an end. The Lean Language
Reference states the danger directly: unrestricted recursion would make Lean's logic
inconsistent, because it would allow a circular proof, one that says a statement holds
because it holds.<ref name="ref-rec">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0
(lean-lang.org, 2026), section 7.6, "Recursive Definitions", with section 7.6.6.1, "Partial
Functions". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/</ref>

== Why Lean cannot just watch for loops ==

A natural idea is to let the computer inspect each definition and decide whether it always
finishes. That cannot be done in general. In 1936 Alan Turing showed that no mechanical
procedure can settle, for every machine, questions of this kind, such as whether a given
machine will ever print a certain symbol.<ref name="turing">A. M. Turing, "On Computable
Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem", ''Proceedings of the London
Mathematical Society'', series 2, vol. 42 (1936–37), pp. 230–265.
doi:10.1112/plms/s2-42.1.230</ref> The best-known form of the result, the '''halting
problem''', asks whether a program stops; it too has no general solution.<ref name="demol">Liesbeth
De Mol, "Turing Machines", ''The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy'' (first published
2018, substantive revision 21 May 2025), section 2.4.
https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-machine/</ref>

So Lean does not try to decide termination. It asks the author for a reason it can check,
and it accepts two kinds of reason.

== Reason one: the input gets smaller ==

Many functions call themselves only on a piece of their input. The factorial is the
standard case:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def fact : Nat → Nat
  | 0     => 1
  | n + 1 => (n + 1) * fact n

#eval fact 20
</pre>

Lean prints <code>2432902008176640000</code>.

A natural number in Lean is zero with some number of "plus ones" stacked on it (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Building things from constructors|building things from
constructors]]). The second line of the definition handles a number of the form
<code>n + 1</code> by calling <code>fact</code> on <code>n</code>, which has one layer fewer.
Every number has finitely many layers, so the calls must reach zero. This is called
'''structural recursion''': each call works on a strict part of the input. Lean recognises
it without help. It translates the definition into the recursion principle that comes with
the type of natural numbers, and the Lean kernel then needs no separate test for termination,
only its ordinary check of types.<ref name="ref-kernel">''The Lean Language Reference'',
version for Lean 4.34.0 (lean-lang.org, 2026), chapter 2, "Elaboration and Compilation",
section 2.3, "The Kernel".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/</ref>

== Reason two: a measure goes down ==

Some functions shrink their input in a way that is not "taking a piece". This one counts how
many times a number can be halved before it falls below 2:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def halvings (n : Nat) : Nat :=
  if n &lt; 2 then 0 else 1 + halvings (n / 2)
termination_by n
decreasing_by omega

#eval halvings 1000
</pre>

Lean prints <code>9</code>.

Half of a number is not one of its layers, so structural recursion does not apply. The line
<code>termination_by n</code> names a '''measure''': a quantity, here the number itself, that
must be smaller at every recursive call. Lean then sets a small proof obligation for each
call. Here the obligation is <code>n / 2 &lt; n</code>, to be shown knowing that
<code>n &lt; 2</code> is false. The line <code>decreasing_by omega</code> supplies the proof,
using an arithmetic procedure described in
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Automation and its limits|automation and its limits]]. When
<code>decreasing_by</code> is left out, Lean tries a default procedure of its own. This is
'''well-founded recursion''': there is no endless descending chain of natural numbers, so a
measure that falls at every step must stop.<ref name="ref-rec" />

The two kinds differ in cost. A function defined by structural recursion computes readily
inside the logic. One defined by well-founded recursion often does not, because the checker
must work through the proof of termination as well; the Lean Language Reference warns that
such functions are frequently slow to compute with (see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Computation inside proofs|computation inside
proofs]]).<ref name="ref-rec" />

== Programs that may never finish ==

Some programs are useful even though nobody can prove that they stop. Start with a positive
whole number; halve it if it is even, otherwise triple it and add one; repeat until you
reach 1. Whether every starting number reaches 1 is the 3x+1 problem, also called the
Collatz problem, and it is unsolved.<ref name="lagarias">Jeffrey C. Lagarias, "The 3x+1
problem: an annotated bibliography (1963–1999) (sorted by author)", arXiv:math/0309224
(2003, revised 2011). https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0309224</ref> A function that counts the
steps can be written, but no proof that it always finishes is known. Lean accepts it when it
is marked <code>partial</code>:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
partial def collatz (n : Nat) : Nat :=
  if n ≤ 1 then 0
  else if n % 2 == 0 then 1 + collatz (n / 2)
  else 1 + collatz (3 * n + 1)

#eval collatz 27
#print collatz
</pre>

The program runs: <code>#eval</code> prints <code>111</code>. But <code>#print</code> shows
what the logic sees: <code>opaque collatz : Nat → Nat</code>. To the logic, a partial
function is a sealed box with the right type and nothing inside. Lean checks that the body
is well typed, compiles it so that it can run, and then keeps only the sealed box for
reasoning.<ref name="ref-rec" /> Even the obvious fact that the count for 1 is 0 cannot be
proved by opening the box:

<pre class="lean lean-cont lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example : collatz 1 = 0 := by rfl
</pre>

Lean replies <code>Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side</code>, then says that
<code>collatz 1</code> "is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side" <code>0</code>.

One condition remains. The result type of a partial function must have at least one value.
Otherwise a partial function promising a value of an empty type could be used to prove a
falsehood, even though it never returns anything.<ref name="ref-rec" /> A definition marked
<code>unsafe</code> drops even that safeguard, and in return no theorem may refer to
it.<ref name="ref-rec" />

== What the rule buys ==

Because of this rule, every function whose definition the logic can use is total: it has an
answer for every input, and the logic may reason about that answer. The price is that the
author must sometimes say why a function stops. That reason is checked like any other proof.
A program that cannot be given one can still be written and run, as <code>partial</code>,
but in proofs it stays a sealed box.
